# Cleaning Oil-Soaked Spark Plugs on a Honda Accord

Finding an inch of pooled oil in the valve cover and spark plug wells of a 1993 Honda Accord is a specific mechanical failure, but it does not automatically mean your engine is destroyed. However, the fact that the car won't turn over suggests a secondary issue likely unrelated to the fouled plugs themselves, which you correctly identified by ruling out the fuel pump. The immediate task is to address the oil contamination on the spark plugs and within the cylinder heads before reassembly.

### Why Oil Fouling Prevents Ignition

Oil leaks into the combustion chamber when the valve cover gasket fails or if the PCV (Positive Crankcase Ventilation) system is overwhelmed. When this happens, oil coats the spark plug electrodes and insulator. Even a thin film of oil creates a conductive path that allows the electrical arc to jump across the gap prematurely or leak down the side of the plug rather than jumping the center electrode to the ground. This results in misfires or a complete inability to ignite the air-fuel mixture.

On your 1993 Accord, if the plugs are completely submerged as you described, they have likely been "wet fouled." Simply wiping them clean with a rag and reinstalling them is insufficient. The oil has penetrated the porous ceramic insulator and coated the metal shell threads. If you attempt to start the engine without addressing this thoroughly, the oil will continue to drip from the valve cover gasket into the wells, causing immediate re-fouling.

### Cleaning Procedure for Soaked Plugs

The cleaning process requires more than just a spray bottle; it needs mechanical agitation and proper solvent choice.

1.  **Remove and Inspect**: You have already removed the plugs. Before cleaning, inspect the spark plug boots on the coil pack or distributor (depending on your specific trim). If the oil has tracked up the outside of the boot, the internal rubber diaphragm may be compromised. In many older Hondas, these boots are cheap enough to replace if they show signs of swelling or cracking from prolonged oil exposure.
2.  **Solvent Selection**: Use a dedicated spark plug cleaner or a mixture of brake cleaner and carburetor cleaner. Avoid gasoline for this task as it leaves residues that can cause deposits when the engine runs hot. Dip each plug into the solvent, ensuring you get into the recessed areas around the threads and the well where the gasket sits.
3.  **Mechanical Agitation**: Scrub the electrodes and insulator tip with a stiff brass wire brush or a dedicated spark plug cleaning tool. Do not use steel wool, as metal shavings can fall into the cylinder head ports. Pay special attention to the area where the plug threads into the block; oil often pools here, leading to rust if not cleaned properly.
4.  **Drying and Inspection**: Allow the plugs to air dry completely in a well-ventilated area. Once dry, inspect the ceramic insulator. If you see deep grooves or pitting from previous misfires caused by the oil, replace the plugs immediately rather than reusing them. Reusing heavily damaged plugs can lead to continued overheating and loss of compression.

### Addressing the Root Cause

Cleaning the plugs is only half the battle. You must address the source of the leak: the valve cover gasket. On a 1993 Accord, these are often made of cork or rubber that degrades over time due to heat cycles. Simply reseating an old gasket will not work; you must replace it with a new OEM-style part.

While cleaning the plugs, also check the spark plug tube seals (often separate from the main valve cover gasket on this model). These small O-rings sit inside the valve cover and prevent oil from dripping down into the wells. If these are hardened or cracked, oil will bypass the new gasket. Replace them along with the main gasket to ensure a permanent fix.

### The "Won't Turn Over" Mystery

It is crucial to note that cleaning the plugs will not solve the fact that your car won't turn over. Since you ruled out the fuel pump, the issue likely lies in the starter motor, the battery connections, or the ignition switch. Oil on the plugs affects combustion, but it does not mechanically prevent the engine from cranking unless the oil has flooded the cylinder so severely that compression is lost entirelyâa scenario less likely if the car simply won't crank at all.

Before reinstalling the cleaned plugs and new gasket, verify the battery voltage and check for corrosion on the starter solenoid terminals. Once the ignition system is mechanically sound and free of oil contamination, you should be able to start the engine successfully.
